DRM controls access and playback (encryption, licences). It does not by itself identify who leaked a copy. Leakers are traced with forensic watermarking, which embeds an invisible viewer- or session-specific mark in the video and is usually deployed alongside DRM. VdoCipher's glossary says DRM 'prevents downloading but cannot attribute a leak once a screen is recorded'.
precise_version: Read more about DRM and forensic watermarking: DRM restricts playback, and a per-viewer watermark is what identifies who leaked a copy.

note: Section 63 of India's Copyright Act, 1957 punishes knowing infringement with 6 months to 3 years' imprisonment plus a fine. In Knit Pro International v. State of NCT of Delhi (20 May 2022), the Supreme Court held the offence cognizable and non-bailable. That is a court ruling, not a government statement. 'Non-bailable' means bail is at the court's discretion, not that it is never granted, and 3 years is the maximum sentence, not a fixed one. Not legal advice; checked 2026-10-13.
precise_version: In India, knowing copyright infringement can carry up to three years' imprisonment, and since 2022 the Supreme Court treats it as a cognizable, non-bailable offence.

Batching per server still helps without repartitioning, because each consumer can sum counts per hashtag within its own batch. A hot hashtag spread over k servers then costs about k writes per batch interval instead of one per post. Partitioning by hashtag makes the aggregation complete and gives each counter a single writer, which avoids contention on hot rows. Kafka Streams does this automatically: groupBy on a new key 'always causes data re-partitioning'.
Correct as stated for this context.

Rejecting Redis Pub/Sub here is right, mainly because of the data-loss point. The cost argument is overstated. Redis channels are not provisioned resources: PUBLISH costs 'O(N+M) where N is the number of clients subscribed to the receiving channel and M the total number of subscribed patterns', so millions of channel names are not inherently expensive. The real problems are at-most-once delivery and push-based flow control (L-0301, L-0302).

Redis Pub/Sub messages are not stored ('at-most-once ... the message is forever lost'), but Redis as a whole does persist data. Its RDB snapshots and AOF log persist the keyspace, and Redis Streams are a persisted log with at-least-once consumer groups.
precise_version: If Redis goes down, Pub/Sub messages in flight are lost, because Redis Pub/Sub does not store messages (Redis Streams do).

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) means using separate models for updates and for reads. Martin Fowler credits the pattern to Greg Young. It does not exist because of Kafka: Fowler notes it 'fits well with event-based programming models' and is often split into services communicating with events. The hashtag document, a read model built asynchronously from events, is a fair CQRS-style example, but the pattern is about separate read and write models, not about Kafka.
precise_version: Building a separate, read-optimised store from events, as the hashtag service does, is in the spirit of CQRS, which separates the write model from the read model; Kafka is a common way to connect the two.

Within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so the partition count is the maximum useful parallelism, not a required worker count. Fewer consumers than partitions also works, with each consumer taking several partitions, and any consumers beyond the partition count sit idle. The Kafka 4.3 javadoc: 'each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group' and the number of threads 'will be limited by the total number of partitions'.
precise_version: The number of consumers that can usefully work in parallel on a topic is at most its number of partitions.

The upheld correction (a replicated Kafka cluster can still go down) is right. The specific 99.9% figure is assessed under L-0313.

Kafka is software, so it has no built-in availability figure. Availability depends on how the cluster is deployed (replication factor, number of AZs, operations), and managed-service SLAs vary. Amazon MSK's SLA gives service credits below 99.9% for Multi-AZ deployments. Confluent Cloud offers 99.99% for multi-zone Standard/Enterprise (2+ eCKU) and Dedicated clusters, 99.95% for single-zone Dedicated, and 99.5% for Basic. The point that Kafka can go down and producers must plan for it stands.
precise_version: Kafka can go down; its availability depends on how the cluster is deployed (managed SLAs range from 99.9% to 99.99%), so producers need a plan for when it is unavailable.

note: Two refinements. First, the Kafka producer already buffers and retries: records wait in up to buffer.memory (default 32 MiB) and are retried until delivery.timeout.ms (default 120 s) before send fails. 'Buffer in memory' is therefore the client's default behaviour for short outages. Second, 'dead letter queue' usually means a place for messages a consumer could not process (SQS moves a message there after maxReceiveCount failed receives). A store for writes that failed to reach Kafka is more precisely a fallback queue or outbox.
Correct: consumer parallelism in a group is bounded by the number of partitions.

Right that few systems give 100% uptime and leader failover costs downtime, but 'two, three seconds' is optimistic as a general figure. AWS says RDS Multi-AZ DB instance 'failover times are typically 60-120 seconds', and clients also need to reconnect and re-resolve DNS. Some systems fail over faster, but plan for tens of seconds or more.
precise_version: Very few systems give 100% uptime; with leader-replica databases you have to bear a failover window, often tens of seconds to a couple of minutes, when the leader goes down.

note: Consistent with how leaderless stores describe themselves: Cassandra's docs call it 'multi-master replication using versioned data', where every replica accepts writes and conflicts are resolved by last-write-wins timestamps.

By default Kafka does not keep messages forever. The broker default is log.retention.hours = 168 (7 days) with log.cleanup.policy = delete, so data older than a week is deleted unless you change it. Keeping data forever needs explicit configuration: retention.ms = -1, or log compaction for keyed latest-value retention. Checked against Kafka 4.1 broker-config docs; the default is unchanged in 4.x.
precise_version: Kafka deletes messages after a retention period (7 days by default); you keep them longer, or forever, only by configuring retention.

note: 'Horizon' is AWS Kinesis vocabulary: TRIM_HORIZON is 'the last untrimmed record in the shard ... the oldest data record in the shard'. Kafka calls this position the earliest offset (log start offset; auto.offset.reset=earliest). Kafka also deletes whole log segments, not individual messages, so the oldest readable record moves forward in segment-sized steps.
Correct: TRIM_HORIZON / earliest means the oldest record still retained, not the first ever written.

Kafka tracks committed offsets per consumer group and partition, not per individual consumer ID. Any member of the group that takes over a partition resumes from the group's committed offset for it. The committed position is 'the offset of the next message to consume', and commitSync 'commits offsets only to Kafka' (stored internally by the broker).
Correct: committing after processing gives at-least-once delivery; after a crash the records since the last commit are processed again.

The three positions are right, but Kafka's default for a brand-new consumer group is the latest offset. auto.offset.reset defaults to 'latest', so a new consumer such as a search indexer starts from new messages and skips existing data unless you set earliest. Kinesis offers the same choices (TRIM_HORIZON, LATEST, AT_SEQUENCE_NUMBER, AT_TIMESTAMP).
Correct as stated for this context.

Kafka's built-in mechanism is tiered storage (KIP-405, production-ready since Kafka 3.9, November 2024). It offloads completed log segments to remote storage such as S3 or HDFS, and consumers can still read them through Kafka; it is not an archive-then-delete step. Kafka ships no RemoteStorageManager implementation ('Kafka server doesn't provide out-of-the-box implementation'), so a plugin is required. Archiving to S3 with a consumer or a Kafka Connect S3 sink, as the teacher describes, is also common.

Finding the bottleneck to raise per-server throughput is optimisation (doing more with the same machine), not vertical scaling. Vertical scaling means moving to a bigger machine with more CPU or RAM. The real choice is horizontal scaling versus vertical scaling versus optimisation, and L-0332 to L-0336 are about optimisation via profiling.
Correct as stated for this context.

Goroutines are cheap ('a few kilobytes' of stack each), so CPU does not limit how many can exist. GOMAXPROCS (default: number of cores) limits how many execute in parallel. Adding CPU helps CPU-bound goroutine work; for I/O-bound goroutines, memory (stacks plus whatever each goroutine holds, like the 20 MB example) or downstream I/O is usually the limit.

The method is good, but 4-byte post IDs are too small at Instagram scale. A 4-byte unsigned INT tops out at 4,294,967,295, so platforms with billions of posts use 64-bit (8-byte, BIGINT) IDs. That makes 100 IDs 800 bytes and a document about 840 bytes, still under 1 KB. The 32-byte tag also assumes ASCII; UTF-8 hashtags in other scripts take more bytes per character.
precise_version: With 64-bit post IDs: 32 B tag + 4 B count + 100 x 8 B IDs = about 836 B, roughly 1 KB per hashtag document.

note: Arithmetic slip: 10^9 hashtags x 0.5 KB = 5 x 10^11 bytes, about 500 GB (half a terabyte), not half a gigabyte. With 64-bit IDs (L-0343) it is closer to 1 TB. That is still manageable on a partitioned store, but it is 1000x the student's figure, which is exactly the thousand-to-billion jump L-0345 warns about. The teacher's reply was a joke, not a correction.
precise_version: A billion half-KB documents is about 500 GB, half a terabyte, not half a gigabyte.

The access-pattern point is right: Kafka cannot look up a record by ID or run queries the way a database can. 'Kafka has no transactions' is wrong, though. Kafka producers use transactions so that writes to several partitions, plus consumer offsets, are committed atomically (exactly-once pipelines). It lacks database-style ACID queries, indexes and point reads.
precise_version: Kafka is not a database: it has no indexes or lookups by key, and its transactions only make a batch of writes atomic, not queries.

note: This is a design opinion, and a common one, but Kafka's creators disagree. Jay Kreps (Confluent, 2017) argues 'there's nothing crazy about storing data in Kafka'. With infinite retention or compaction, Kafka can be the system of record for event-sourced designs, which 'does mean raising the bar for how you run it'. For lookups by ID (L-0352) a database is still needed.

Kafka itself has no broker-side DLQ. Kafka Connect does provide one: errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name is 'the topic to be used as the dead letter queue (DLQ) for messages that result in an error'. SQS's DLQ feature also catches messages consumers failed to process ('messages that are not processed successfully'), not failed writes to another system. To hold writes that failed to reach Kafka, you write them to a plain SQS queue (or another store) used as a fallback, not to an SQS DLQ.
precise_version: If a write to Kafka fails, you can write it to a separate fallback queue such as SQS and re-ingest it later; SQS works well for this.

note: This is not the transactional outbox pattern. In the outbox pattern the service always writes the message to an outbox table 'as part of the transaction that updates the business entities', and a separate relay then publishes it to the broker. That makes the DB write and the event atomic and avoids the dual-write problem. Writing to the DB only after a Kafka write fails is a fallback store and keeps the dual-write problem: a crash between the two writes still loses the message.
precise_version: Writing failed messages to your own database and replaying them later is a fallback store. The transactional outbox pattern goes further: every message is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business data, and a relay publishes it.

The list mixes categories. Kafka and Kinesis are transport/log systems, not compute frameworks. Flume is 'a distributed ... service for efficiently collecting, aggregating, and moving large amounts of log data'. The distributed-compute options for the counting step are Spark (which has Kafka connectors), Flink, Kafka Streams and similar.
